abstract: The kidney connecting tubule lies between the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct. Even though short, it plays a key role in regulating calcium, sodium, and potassium excretion and water balance in health and disease. In rodents and humans, transitions between distal segments are gradual, making the assignment of functional properties to cell types difficult. To address this, we enriched mouse kidney distal tubule cells prior to performing single nucleus RNA-sequencing. Connecting tubule cells separated into three clusters, one expressed genes that are relevant to calcium transport, while another expressed genes that are relevant to water transport. The third was intermediate between the other two. While genes for electrogenic sodium transport were expressed throughout the connecting tubule, Hsd11b2, the gene responsible for aldosterone-responsiveness, was expressed primarily by the distal cluster. Immunocytochemistry confirmed the separation of calcium and water transport pathways and spatial transcriptomics confirmed the linear organization of this segment. Human transcriptomic data showed similar gene separation. The results show that rodent and human connecting tubules separate calcium and water transport, thereby limiting tubule fluid calcium accumulation. They also restrict aldosterone action to segments that are responsive to arginine vasopressin to maintain sodium homeostasis during antidiuresis.
